item.title: [The Lancet] [Editorial] Multiple sclerosis: beyond controlling relapses
item.description: Few neurological diseases have seen a transformation in diagnosis and treatment as remarkable as multiple sclerosis. A chronic, heterogeneous autoimmune condition, it typically begins in early adulthood and affects over 3 million people, with women roughly three times more likely to be affected than men. Characterised by inflammation, demyelination, axonal injury, and neuronal loss, multiple sclerosis can cause relapses and gradual accumulation of disability. Three decades ago, treatment options were few and far between; today, more than 20 disease-modifying therapies are available.

item.description: Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitors directly modulate the functions of B lymphocytes and myeloid cells (notably macrophages and microglia) and thus target both the adaptive and innate mechanisms that contribute to the immunopathology of multiple sclerosis on either side of the blood–brain barrier. item.title: [The Lancet] [Comment] Expanding the post-EGFR TKI landscape with antibody–drug conjugates
item.description: Third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), increasingly combined with chemotherapy or amivantamab, are the preferred front-line treatment for EGFR-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC).1,2 With actionable resistance mechanisms often absent at progression, effective second-line therapies are needed.3 Antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) offer one such approach, although randomised trials have yielded variable results.4–6

item.title: [The Lancet] [Comment] Offline: A manifesto for protecting public health
item.description: Public health institutions are being threatened by political attack. Governments that dislike being held accountable for their public health responsibilities deploy multiple means to undermine these institutions. At the European Public Health Conference, held in Bilbao, Spain, last week, Christina Pagel explained how. Contesting the science by challenging its rigour. Moving decisions from experts to political appointees. Linking funding and job security to obsequious compliance. Suppressing evidence.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Perspectives] Monica Geingos: advocate for adolescent health joins PMNCH
item.description: “Sexual and reproductive health and rights [SRHR] have been under a constant and coordinated attack”, notes Monica Geingos, former First Lady of Namibia, UNAIDS Special Ambassador for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights, and Co-Chair of the UNAIDS Global Council on Inequality, AIDS and Pandemics. This month, Geingos brought her wide-ranging expertise to a new role as Board Chair of the Partnership for Maternal, Newborn and Child Health (PMNCH). Her leadership comes at a challenging time.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Perspectives] What do artists know?
item.description: Until the day my newborn son died, I worked as an artist. I spent each day in the studio making drawings and films, over 15 years preparing work for exhibitions, commissions, and eventually a doctorate in fine art. After he died (in my arms, peacefully, not unexpectedly), I directed everything I had learned as an artist into writing the story of his birth and death. As it turned out, over those years in the studio I had developed aptitudes well matched to drawing meaning from experience too adverse to bear.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] Agatha Christie: medicine, diagnosis, and the art of detection
item.description: 2026 marks the 50th anniversary of the death of Agatha Christie (1890–1976). item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] The F-words for Child Development: Lessons Learned
item.description: We write as the creators and promoters of the F-words for Child Development framework1 to thank Chloe Wilson and colleagues for their refreshing advocacy of this expanded set of ideas regarding disability.2 Not surprisingly, we agree with and fully endorse the concepts being promoted.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] Disability-inclusive research: operational challenges
item.description: Chloe Wilson and colleagues have recently provided author guidance on reporting disability.1 We congratulate the authors for acknowledging the diversity in the experience of disability.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] The Lancet Group's guidance on reporting disability: make link to the ICF explicit

item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] Defining success in kidney xenotransplantation
item.description: Leonardo V Riella and colleagues report the first successful transition from porcine kidney xenotransplantation to allotransplantation.1 The possibility of this bridge raises important questions about its purpose and how its success should be defined—traditionally by graft survival.2 Xenotransplantation could serve different purposes, including reducing time on dialysis for patients waiting for an allograft, decreasing waiting-list mortality, or providing an alternative for patients unlikely to receive an allograft.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] Defining success in kidney xenotransplantation – Authors' reply
item.description: We thank Christopher H Kim and colleagues for their thoughtful comments and agree that success in kidney xenotransplantation should ultimately extend beyond graft survival or dialysis independence alone. Their Correspondence highlights an important question as the field transitions from individual first-in-human experiences to prospective clinical trials.

item.description: Ginn S. Richard Dadd's beguiling art. item.title: [British Journal of Anaesthesia] Delayed residual gastric contents in adolescents receiving glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists. Comment on Br J Anaesth 2026; 137: 1507–13
item.description: We read with interest the prospective cohort study by O'Brien and colleagues1 examining residual gastric contents in fasted adolescents receiving glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs). The inclusion of an at-risk non-user group provides an important opportunity to examine the contribution of medication exposure alongside underlying metabolic diseases.

item.title: [British Journal of Anaesthesia] Socioeconomic status and mortality after acute hip fracture surgery in Sweden: educational attainment, frailty, and the causal interpretation of mortality. Comment on Br J Anaesth 2026; 137: 1136–45
item.description: We read with interest the nationwide registry study by Åhman and colleagues,1 which linked individual-level socioeconomic status measures to 30-day and 2-yr mortality after acute hip fracture surgery in 58 641 patients in Sweden. The educational gradient in long-term mortality was particularly notable: compared with >12 yr of education, <9 yr of education was associated with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.25 for 2-yr mortality and an adjusted absolute risk difference of 6.3%. These findings are important because they demonstrate persistent outcome inequality despite universal healthcare and stand

item.title: [British Journal of Anaesthesia] Impact of high versus low fraction of inspired oxygen for anaesthetic washout and extubation on postoperative pulmonary atelectasis formation and oxygenation: fraction of inspired oxygen and postoperative pulmonary atelectasis. Comment on Br J Anaesth 2026; 137: 591–600
item.description: We read with interest the randomised controlled trial by Paschold and colleagues1 investigating the effects of different fractions of inspired oxygen (Fio2s) administered during anaesthetic washout and tracheal extubation on postoperative atelectasis and oxygenation. The authors are to be commended for addressing an underexplored component of perioperative lung protection. Their use of electrical impedance tomography (EIT) allowed dynamic assessment of regional ventilation and end-expiratory lung volume (EELV) during the transition from controlled ventilation to spontaneous breathing.
